common_name: Little Lemons Clematis (Dwarf Golden-Bell Tangutica Clematis)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level; this compact tangutica selection breaks dormancy later than most clematis, so avoid disturbing it in early spring.

directions: Little Lemons is a dwarf, late-breaking selection of the golden-bell species Clematis tangutica, staying compact enough for a large patio pot or the front of a mixed border instead of scrambling skyward like its parent. Nodding, lantern-shaped soft yellow flowers appear in flushes from late spring into early autumn, followed by the same silky silver seed heads that make tangutica types valuable for two seasons of interest. Because it flowers on new growth, cut all stems back hard to a few inches above the base in late winter; the plant tolerates hot, dry sites and drought better than most clematis once established. Give it well-drained soil and avoid overwatering in winter, when the crown is prone to rot if left soggy.

common_name: Margaret Hunt Clematis (Dusky Mauve-Pink Summer-to-Autumn Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring, setting the crown a couple of inches below soil level and shading the roots with a low companion plant while the vine climbs into sun.

directions: Raised by Fisk's Clematis Nursery and introduced in 1969, Margaret Hunt is a vigorous late bloomer valued for carrying its dusky mauve-pink flowers from midsummer well into autumn, long after most large-flowered hybrids have finished. Each four-inch flower opens with a slightly darker bar down the center of the petals that fades to a soft pearly pink as it ages, giving the whole plant a two-toned look over a long season. Because it flowers entirely on the current year's growth, cut all stems back hard to within a foot of the ground in late winter to keep its vigorous habit in check and maximize bloom. It tolerates any aspect and rewards rich, moisture-retentive soil with an extra-long flowering season.

common_name: Yukiokoshi Clematis (Japanese Ragged Double White Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, well-drained soil with the crown a couple of inches deep; give some afternoon shade in hot climates to protect the delicate white blooms.

directions: A heritage Japanese selection of Clematis patens, Yukiokoshi produces irregular, almost shredded-looking double white flowers brushed with pale green at the base of the tepals on its first spring flush, followed by a lighter, more conventional second flush on new growth in late summer. Because it blooms on old wood in spring, only tidy and shape the vine right after the first flush, removing dead or crossing stems rather than cutting it hard back. Give it a position with some afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the ragged white blooms from bleaching, and mulch to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist.

common_name: Bredon Blue Clematis (Mid-Blue Bell-Flowered Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in spring in sharply drained soil; this Atragene-group hybrid tolerates a shaded or north-facing fence as readily as full sun.

directions: Bredon Blue is an Atragene-group hybrid prized for its nodding, bell-shaped mid-blue flowers with a frilly creamy-white inner skirt, carried in abundance over a compact, wiry vine in mid-spring. Like other alpina and macropetala relatives it flowers only on growth made the previous year, so it needs no routine pruning beyond a light tidy immediately after flowering to remove dead or damaged stems and keep it within bounds. It thrives in poor, sharply drained soil and tolerates a shaded or north-facing fence as readily as full sun, making it a useful choice for difficult cold corners. Decorative fluffy seed heads follow the spring bloom and persist into summer.

common_name: Astra Nova Clematis (Semi-Double Violet-Purple Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; compact enough growth suits a large container as well as a fence or obelisk.

directions: Bred by the Jan van Zoest nursery in Holland from a 2006 cross and introduced in 2009, Astra Nova is a semi-double viticella hybrid whose violet-purple tepals are brightened by a central white stripe and a spiky center of petal-like stamens. It blooms continuously from early summer through autumn, one of the longest flowering windows in the viticella group, on growth compact enough to suit a large container as well as an obelisk or fence. As with other viticella types, cut all growth back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter; the vigorous new shoots that follow will carry the entire season's flowers. It is exceptionally disease-resistant and forgiving, making it a reliable choice for beginner gardeners.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; this vigorous, easy-care vine tolerates any aspect.

directions: Forever Friends was bred by Wim Snoeijer at the Jan van Zoest nursery and introduced through Thorncroft Clematis, who named it in memory of the breeder's father. Satin-white, star-shaped flowers around three inches across, each centered with contrasting dusky-red anthers, open in flushes from midsummer into autumn on a vigorous, easy-care vine. It flowers entirely on the current season's growth, so prune all stems back hard to within a foot of the ground in late winter to encourage the strongest flush of new flowering wood. Unscented but exceptionally free-flowering, it tolerates any aspect and is a dependable choice for covering a fence or arbor quickly.

common_name: Petit Faucon Clematis (Non-Clinging Bluey-Purple Scrambling Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in spring in average, well-drained soil; its stems lack true clinging tendrils, so give it a small shrub, obelisk with ties, or large container to scramble through.

directions: Bred by Raymond Evison and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, Petit Faucon is a semi-herbaceous diversifolia hybrid with nodding to outward-facing, rich bluey-purple flowers set off by rosy-purple filaments and golden anthers. Because its stems do not produce true clinging tendrils, it behaves more like a scrambling perennial than a climber, best grown through a small shrub, up an obelisk with ties, or trailing from a large container. It flowers continuously from late spring through September on new growth, so cut the whole plant back hard to six to eight inches in late winter to renew it for the coming season. Average, well-drained soil and any aspect short of deep shade will keep it flowering steadily all summer.

common_name: Jacqueline du Pré Clematis (Nodding Mauve-Pink Early Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches deep; tolerates a cooler, shadier fence or trellis better than most large-flowered hybrids.

directions: Raised by Barry Fretwell at Peveril Clematis Nursery in Devon and named for the celebrated cellist, Jacqueline du Pré is an Atragene-group hybrid bearing nodding, semi-double, pale mauve-pink bells with a deeper pink reverse in mid- to late spring. Like other alpina and macropetala relatives it flowers on stems made the previous year, so prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead wood and control size rather than cutting it back hard. It is reliably winter-hardy and tolerates a shadier fence or trellis better than most large-flowered hybrids, making it a dependable choice for a cool, north-facing wall. Decorative, fluffy seed heads follow the spring bloom and add interest into early summer.

common_name: Orange Peel Clematis (Thick-Petaled Golden Bell Species Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; give it a sturdy large shrub, pergola, or fence to scramble through.

directions: Selected from the Himalayan species Clematis tibetana, Orange Peel is named for the unusually thick, waxy texture of its nodding, lantern-shaped yellow flowers, whose pebbled surface genuinely recalls the rind of a citrus fruit. Blooms open from midsummer through early autumn, each with a prominent cluster of dark stamens, followed by the large, silvery, fluffy seed heads typical of the tibetana-tangutica complex that persist into winter. It is a vigorous climber best given a sturdy large shrub, pergola, or fence to scramble through, and because it flowers only on the current season's growth it can be cut back hard to the base every late winter. Site it in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates poor, dry ground better than most clematis once established.
